results.title: CoreWeave Raised Prices by 25 Percent. Its Near-Term Computing Capacity Is Still Effectively Sold Out
highlights:
# CoreWeave Raised Prices by 25 Percent. Its Near-Term Computing Capacity Is Still Effectively Sold Out

The AI infrastructure shortage is allowing old chips to remain valuable and pushing customers to pay premiums for near-term capacity. 

BY GEORGIA FEARN, EDITORIAL INTERN

Aug 12, 2026

Photo: Getty Images

CoreWeave says its near-term AI computing capacity is effectively sold out. That announcement comes after it raised prices across its product lineup by roughly 25 percent in July.

Rival AI cloud provider Nebius said Wednesday that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity today on terms similar to its latest deals, but it is deliberately holding some back for immediate customer needs. According to the company, shorter contracts can often command even higher prices.

Customers are paying premiums for near-term computing power, new contracts are becoming more profitable, and even older generations of Nvidia GPUs—the chips used to train and run AI models—are still commanding strong prices years after newer chips arrive.

CoreWeave co-founder and CEO Michael Intrator said contracts signed last quarter are expected to carry contribution margins five to 10 percentage points higher than those signed in recent quarters. Customers, he said, are increasingly making money from their AI products and are more willing to pay for the compute that’s needed to grow.

The demand is showing up in CoreWeave’s numbers. Second-quarter revenue more than doubled to $2.58 billion, while revenue backlog reached roughly $104 billion, excluding more than $25 billion of additional commitments signed early in the third quarter.

“Pricing is extremely strong on short term deals,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Vasu Kasibhotla told Inc. Wednesday. Nebius, he noted, is now citing roughly $40 million in annual contract value per megawatt of data center power for short-term capacity, “materially higher than the $10-15 million the market expected just a year ago.”

## Prices keep climbing

Nebius entered 2026 with baseline annual contract value of about $12 million per megawatt. Its second-quarter deals averaged more than $20 million. It now sees an opportunity to charge $40 million to $50 million per megawatt for three-to-six-month deals.

results.title: The Most Important AI Demand Data Available | Investing.com
highlights:
Hyperscalers tell us how much they plan to spend. Chip and equipment vendors tell us what is shipping. But neoclouds show whether customers are actually renting infrastructure, at what prices, and for how long. CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) just provided the most important demand-side confirmation the AI cycle has produced.

CoreWeave’s revenue surged 112% year-over-year to $2.58 billion. Adjusted EBITDA reached $1.51 billion at a 59% margin. Management projected an $18.5-19.5 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end. The forward indicators are even more telling: CoreWeave finished Q2 with $104 billion of backlog, up 246% year-over-year, and then added more than $25 billion of net-new commitments in early Q3. Pricing was raised 25% in July. New contracts carry contribution margins 5-10 percentage points above recent deals. Even older A100 hardware has been extended through 2029. Capacity is selling out immediately upon deployment.

Nebius was growing even faster: revenue soared 454% to $582 million. Annualized run-rate revenue jumped 56% sequentially to $3 billion. Adjusted EBITDA reached $236 million at a 41% margin. The neocloud signed four AI-cloud agreements averaging more than $1 billion each. Its first capacity auction cleared 15% above the previous record price. Management said it could sell all planned 2027 capacity today. Backlog exceeded $40 billion.

Both companies said the same thing: newly deployed capacity sells out immediately, and the constraint is physical supply — power, land, equipment delivery — not customer demand or customer willingness to pay. Pricing is strengthening, not requiring discounting. Commitments are extending further into the future with every quarter.

The neocloud model is also validating itself as something more than a GPU rental business. CoreWeave’s non-GPU products exceed $400 million of ARR. Managed Inference ARR exploded from $1 million to more than $100 million in a few months and should reach $250 million by year-end. Nebius is pursuing the same evolution through Token Factory and Tavily. Both are becoming full-stack AI platforms, not commodity compute providers. That evolution creates stickier customer relationships and better economics, while further raising the competitive moat against the hyperscalers they supposedly compete with.

results.title: Nebius Earnings: GPU Spot Prices Triple and Neoclouds Exploit Short-Term Scarcity | Morningstar
highlights:
Our key takeaways from Nebius Group’s NBIS second-quarter call are that GPU spot rental rates continue to climb as the artificial intelligence supply/demand imbalance intensifies and neoclouds want to maximize value extracted from short-term pricing.

Why it matters: Average contract value per megawatt has more than tripled in the year to date, from an average of $12 million/MW in early 2026 to $20 million/MW in the second quarter, and some third-quarter contracts are being signed at $40 million/MW. We think management is avoiding long-term capacity commitments, favoring three-to-six-month contracts, as it believes GPU spot rates will continue to climb, allowing a massive pricing tailwind in late 2026 and 2027.

- Quarterly revenue grew 454% to $582 million with a negative 30% operating margin. We estimate higher-priced contracts will have a significant positive impact on profitability in late 2026 and 2027. This massive pricing tailwind is supply/demand driven, not driven by any durable differentiation, and we remain cautious about assuming such pricing persists into perpetuity. Once the imbalance eases, the pricing situation would play in reverse.

The bottom line: We raise our fair value estimate for no-moat Nebius to $150 from $120, reflecting higher GPU rental prices in the next three years, improving operating margins, and reducing the free cash flow burn. We estimate Nebius will burn close to $30 billion in free cash flow in the next five years, requiring continued equity and debt raises.

results.title: Power and Cooling Are the New GPU Shortage: Inside the Data Center Bottleneck - Data Storage
highlights:
> A GPU order placed today can ship in weeks. The transformer that feeds it can take two years. That gap, not chip allocation, is what now decides when your cluster comes online. 

For three years the industry told a single story about scarcity: there were not enough accelerators, and whoever held allocation held the market. That story is going stale. Supply of high-end accelerators has loosened at the margins, secondary capacity is being resold, and buyers who once waited months for a quote now get three of them in a week. What has not loosened is everything underneath the chip. Grid interconnection, on-site substations, switchgear, chillers, and liquid-ready white space have all become harder to get than the silicon they exist to serve.

This matters to anyone signing a compute contract, because the constraint has moved somewhere your procurement process probably does not look. You can diligence a provider's GPU inventory in an afternoon. Diligencing whether they actually control the megawatts to run it takes different questions entirely.

...

Aggregate numbers understate the problem, because demand is not spread evenly. It clusters in a handful of markets with fiber density, tax treatment, and existing campuses: Northern Virginia, Dallas, Phoenix, Columbus, and a short list of European and Nordic equivalents. Those are precisely the markets where utilities have stopped quoting fast interconnection dates. The result is a market where the accelerator is available and the place to plug it in is not.

...

The density curve is the mechanism behind all of this. A conventional enterprise rack in 2022 drew 5 to 10 kW and was cooled with air, in a hall designed around that assumption. An 8-way H100 node draws roughly 10.2 kW on its own, so a single node now consumes the power budget of an entire legacy rack. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72, a rack-scale system with 72 GPUs in one liquid-cooled enclosure, draws on the order of 120 kW.

...

Efficiency has been flat while all this happened. The Uptime Institute's 2024 global survey put the average reported PUE at about 1.56, essentially unchanged for several years, because the fleet average is dominated by older halls, not by the handful of new hyperscale builds achieving far better numbers. That flat industry average is the number that lands on your invoice when you rent from an operator running legacy floor space.

...

Behind the facility sits the grid, and the grid has a queue. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Queued Up series has tracked well over 2,000 GW of generation and storage capacity waiting in United States interconnection queues, with typical waits from request to commercial operation measured in years rather than months. Large load interconnection, which is what a new campus needs, sits in an adjacent process that is no faster.

Equipment lead times compound it. High-voltage transformers, switchgear, and gas turbines have all been quoted at multi-year deliveries since the 2023 demand surge, and the manufacturing base for them expands slowly because the buyers are utilities with long capital cycles. None of this responds to a compute buyer's urgency.

The practical effect for buyers is a widening gap between providers who already hold energized capacity and providers who hold a signed land deal and a utility study. Both can put a 2027 date on a slide. Only one of them controls whether that date holds.

...

## What power actually costs you per GPU hour

It is worth converting megawatts into the unit you actually buy in. Take a 1,000-GPU H100 cluster built from 8-way nodes at 10.2 kW each. That is 125 nodes and roughly 1,275 kW of IT load. At the industry average PUE of 1.56, facility draw is about 1,989 kW, which works out to almost exactly 2.0 kWh of facility energy per GPU hour.

At 8 cents per kWh, a competitive industrial rate in a low-cost market, that is 16 cents per GPU hour in electricity alone. At 20 cents per kWh, a realistic rate in a constrained metro, it is 40 cents. Against on-demand H100 rental prices that have been trading in the low single dollars per hour, power alone can be a tenth to a fifth of the sell price before anyone has paid for the GPU, the building, the network, or the staff.

Now change one variable. A modern liquid-cooled hall running at a PUE of 1.10 instead of 1.56 drops facility energy to about 1.40 kWh per GPU hour. On a 1,000-GPU cluster at 14 cents per kWh, that difference is roughly 736,000 dollars a year, for identical GPUs doing identical work. Efficiency and location are not facility trivia. They are a line item large enough to swing a build versus rent decision on their own.

DataStorage.com original analysis: electricity cost per H100 GPU hour

| Electricity rate | PUE 1.56 | PUE 1.10 | Annual delta, 1,000 GPUs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 cents per kWh | $0.160 | $0.112 | $420,000 |
| 14 cents per kWh | $0.280 | $0.196 | $736,000 |
| 20 cents per kWh | $0.400 | $0.280 | $1,051,000 |

Model assumes 125 eight-way nodes at 10.2 kW, 1,275 kW IT load, continuous operation for 8,760 hours. Facility energy rounds to 2.0 kWh per GPU hour at PUE 1.56 and 1.40 kWh at PUE 1.10, and every figure derives from those two rounded values.

...

If power is billed as a pass-through, the difference between 1.15 and 1.45 is money moving directly from you to the utility.

### Ask how power is priced in the contract

All-in dollars per GPU hour, dollars per kW-month plus metered energy, and pass-through at cost plus a margin behave completely differently when tariffs move. Only one of the three leaves the price risk with the provider. Know which one you signed, and model your spend both ways in a cloud cost calculator before committing to a term.

...

### Prefer shorter terms in constrained markets, longer terms where power is abundant

Where capacity is scarce, prices are high and the market is moving, so optionality is worth paying for. Where power is genuinely abundant and the operator controls it, a longer commitment buys a rate you will not beat later. Match contract length to the local power situation, not to a blanket procurement policy, and price the alternatives the way you would when weighing reserved, on-demand and spot instances.

## Key takeaways

Key Takeaways

- Chip allocation has loosened faster than the facilities that host chips. Energized, liquid-ready capacity is now the binding constraint on most deployment timelines.
- Rack density rose ten to fifteen times in one hardware generation. A 120 kW rack-scale system cannot be retrofitted into a hall designed for 8 kW racks by adding cooling.
- Above roughly 30 to 50 kW per rack, direct-to-chip liquid cooling is mandatory, and it brings a facility water loop, CDU redundancy, and failure modes measured in minutes.
- Power alone runs 16 to 40 cents per H100 GPU hour depending on rate and efficiency. A PUE of 1.10 versus 1.56 is worth about 736,000 dollars a year on a 1,000-GPU cluster.
- Ask providers for contracted load, annualized measured PUE, and the power pricing mechanism. Installed capacity and design PUE are marketing numbers.

## FAQ

Is the GPU shortage over in 2026?

The acute shortage of high-end accelerators has eased at the margins, with secondary capacity being resold and quote turnaround measured in days rather than months. The shortage has moved down the stack instead. Grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, and liquid-ready white space are now harder to secure than the chips themselves, so deployment timelines are set by facilities rather than by allocation.

...

For an H100 cluster built from 10.2 kW eight-way nodes, facility energy is about 2.0 kWh per GPU hour at the industry average PUE of 1.56, and about 1.40 kWh per GPU hour at a modern PUE of 1.10. That translates to 16 cents per GPU hour at 8 cents per kWh and 40 cents at 20 cents per kWh, before any other cost is counted.

...

In constrained metros where prices are elevated and capacity is moving, shorter terms preserve the option to reprice as new supply energizes. In markets with genuinely abundant power held by an operator that controls its own substation, a longer term locks a rate that is unlikely to improve. Match the contract length to the local power situation rather than to a blanket policy.

results.title: Nvidia Blackwell Prices Surge 48%, Forcing AI Firms to Ration Services
highlights:
Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs have seen a significant price increase of 48% within two months due to high demand and capacity constraints, compelling AI companies to limit their services. This development underscores the growing challenges in meeting the computational needs of advanced AI systems.

...

The price of Nvidia’s highly sought-after Blackwell GPUs has surged dramatically, rising from $2.75 to $4.08 per hour over the past two months. This 48% increase is largely driven by a constrained supply of GPU resources amid a surge in demand from AI firms deploying powerful, large-scale AI systems. The rise in prices reflects the growing computational needs as companies race to develop and scale agentic AI technologies. 

The shortage of computing power is causing ripple effects across the industry, with many companies now forced to ration their AI services. Smaller firms and startups, in particular, are struggling to compete for limited GPU resources, potentially stalling innovation in certain areas. Meanwhile, larger corporations with more resources may gain an advantage, further exacerbating the gap between industry players.

Why it matters

The sharp rise in GPU rental costs could slow down advancements in AI by limiting access to computational resources, particularly for smaller companies. This may lead to greater consolidation in the AI industry as well-funded firms gain a competitive edge. Supply chain and resource constraints could also push governments and private sectors to invest in alternative computing solutions.

...

To contextualize, Nvidia's position in the AI hardware market has become analogous to OPEC's role in global oil markets during the 1970s. Just as oil was the lifeblood of industrial economies, GPUs are now the lifeblood of AI innovation. The explosive growth of generative AI, large language models, and agentic AI systems has outstripped the capacity of hardware manufacturers to supply adequate computational resources. Nvidia, which commands roughly 80% of the GPU market, is uniquely positioned to capitalize on this demand spike, but it also concentrates risk in the hands of one company. Historically, such monopolistic dynamics often lead to price volatility, supply disruptions, and a chilling effect on smaller players unable to compete.

results.title: A GPU from 2020 just sold at full price through 2029 · Stacks
highlights:
Reporting second-quarter results on August 11, CoreWeave said it had signed a contract on NVIDIA's A100, a chip from 2020, that runs to 2029, at full price. In the same call it said it had raised rental prices across its lineup by about 25% in July.

That report notes the increase came in two layers. The 25% raised against demand is one, and a pass-through of higher hardware costs sits on top of it.

...

When a company buys $10 billion of equipment it does not book $10 billion of cost that year. It spreads the cost across the years it expects to use the gear. That is depreciation. One more step shows why this touches the share price. Stretch the number of years and the cost booked each year falls, which makes that year's profit look larger. How many years a company writes down for its equipment therefore sets the size of its reported profit. Michael Burry aimed at exactly this in November 2025. He argued that hyperscalers were understating depreciation by $176 billion across 2026 to 2028 by extending useful lives, and that this inflated Oracle's profit by 26.9% and Meta's by 20.8%.

...

The A100 launched in May 2020. A contract running to 2029 is nine years from that date. Chief executive Mike Intrator said the deal was struck at full freight, meaning without a discount, and the finance chief said average selling prices on older generations are at or above where they sat a year ago. The same release put second-quarter revenue at $2.575 billion, up 112% from a year earlier, with $104 billion of contracted work not yet recognised as revenue. Active power rose by about 500 megawatts during the quarter to 1.5 gigawatts, and the year-end target was raised above 1.85 gigawatts. All of these figures are CoreWeave's own disclosures. Who signed the contract, and what the price actually is, were not made public.

GPUs lose usefulness within three or four years and leave nothing at resale, so stretching their book life inflates profit.

If somebody still wants to rent the older gear, it carries a price. Older-generation ASPs are running above last year.

The owner who runs the chip and the landlord who rents it out are reading different values off the same silicon.

...

This is why a single contract does not settle it. CoreWeave is paid by the hour to run other people's compute, so an older chip pays as long as it stays booked. Meta and Oracle are using the gear to train their own models. When a newer chip does more work on the same electricity, the older one can be cheaper left idle. The same chip in a different seat is worth a different amount. There is one thing to watch. If more companies follow Amazon and shorten the life, CoreWeave's contract stays a fact about the rental business. If more follow Meta and stretch it, the reading that old GPUs still carry a price gets stronger.

results.title: CME Group Sets 5 October Launch for Compute Futures as GPU Rental Costs Become a Hedgeable Risk
highlights:
CME Group and GPU market intelligence and benchmarking firm Silicon Data have announced plans to launch two Compute futures contracts on 5 October 2026, subject to regulatory review. The contracts will give AI developers, cloud operators and investors a regulated way to hedge the cost of processing power, an input that has moved from a line item in a technology budget to one of the largest variable costs in the global economy.

Silicon Data H100 Rental Index Futures and Silicon Data B200 Rental Index Futures will track indices measuring hourly GPU rental costs published by Silicon Data, which is backed by global trading firm DRW. Each contract represents a month's worth of rent for the Nvidia H100, the chip at the centre of the current AI build out, and the next generation Nvidia Blackwell B200 respectively. The contracts are cash settled against the indices rather than involving any physical delivery of hardware, and will be listed under the rules of NYMEX. 

#### An input that has never had a public price

Renting AI compute has until now been a matter of private negotiation, with prices varying widely by provider, contract length and demand conditions.

> "For years, two companies buying the exact same GPU capacity could pay wildly different prices with no way to know who got the better deal. They will now have a benchmark to check that against." - Carmen Li, Chief Executive Officer, Silicon Data

Li added that the contracts give the market a public, tradable reference price for the resource every AI system runs on, turning compute from something enterprises negotiate blindly into something they can plan around.

...

The venue that captures early liquidity is likely to set the global reference price for compute, much as ICE Brent and CME WTI did in oil, while fragmented rival contracts risk splitting activity across platforms and leaving none of them deep enough to be useful.

...

Until now, a firm wanting exposure to, or protection from, the cost of AI infrastructure has had to express it through proxies such as chipmaker equity or cloud provider earnings. A listed contract on rental cost gives a direct hedge instead, and once the contracts are live, trading platforms will be able to add them to their product suites.

highlights:
#### 코어위브, 2분기 실적 발표 계기 재조명 AI 훈련·추론 수요 폭증…자체 데이터센터만으론 공급 한계 코어위브, 메타 210억달러 추가 계약…수주잔고 1040억달러 매출 112% 급증에 주가 시간외 14%↑…올 최대 390억달러 투자

 

마이클 인트레이터 코어위브(CoreWeave) 창립자 겸 CEO./로이터연합

생성형 인공지능(AI) 경쟁이 '모델 성능'에서 이를 구동할 컴퓨팅 자원 확보전으로 확산하면서 코어위브(CoreWeave)와 같은 그래픽처리장치(GPU) 전문 클라우드 업체의 몸값이 치솟고 있다.

메타(Meta) 등 대형 기술기업조차 자체 데이터센터만으로 폭증하는 AI 모델 훈련과 추론 수요를 감당하기 어려워지면서 외부 GPU 인프라 확보에 수십억~수백억달러를 투입하고 있다.

AI 데이터센터 공급이 빠르게 늘어나고 있음에도 엔비디아(Nvidia)의 최신 GPU 임대 가격과 마진이 오히려 최고치를 경신하고 있다는 점도 AI 컴퓨팅 자원을 둘러싼 공급 부족이 여전히 이어지고 있음을 보여준다.

이 같은 수요를 등에 업은 코어위브는 올해 2분기 매출이 전년 동기보다 112% 급증하고 수주잔고가 1040억달러까지 불어났다.

실적이 시장 예상을 웃돌면서 코어위브 주가는 11일(현지시간) 미국 증시 시간외 거래에서 14% 급등했다.

...

하지만 시장이 주목한 것은 현재 손익보다 폭발적으로 증가하는 AI 컴퓨팅 수요와 이를 바탕으로 쌓이고 있는 장기 계약이었다.

코어위브의 매출 수주잔고는 2분기 말 기준 1040억달러까지 확대됐다.

여기에는 올해 3분기 들어 새롭게 확보한 250억달러 이상의 계약 약정도 포함되지 않았다.

향후 매출로 전환될 계약 물량이 이미 현재 연간 매출의 여러 배에 달하는 가운데 추가 계약까지 이어지고 있는 셈이다.

...

코어위브의 성장 배경에는 빅테크를 중심으로 한 AI 컴퓨팅 자원 확보 경쟁이 자리 잡고 있다.

생성형 AI 시장 초기에는 대규모언어모델(LLM)을 개발하기 위한 '훈련' 수요가 GPU 시장을 이끌었다면 AI 서비스가 본격적으로 확산하면서 실제 이용자의 질문에 답하거나 이미지·영상 등을 생성하는 '추론' 수요까지 빠르게 늘고 있다.

대규모 AI 모델을 개발하고 운영하기 위해 필요한 GPU 수요가 동시에 증가하면서 자체 데이터센터를 보유한 글로벌 기술기업들조차 필요한 컴퓨팅 자원을 제때 확보하기 어려워지는 상황이다.

코어위브는 이런 공급 부족을 파고든 대표적인 GPU 전문 클라우드 사업자다.

아마존과 구글, 마이크로소프트(MS) 등 기존 클라우드 업체와 달리 엔비디아 GPU를 기반으로 AI 연산 인프라를 집중적으로 구축해 이를 필요한 기업에 임대하는 방식으로 사업을 빠르게 확대하고 있다.

대형 기술기업들이 자체 데이터센터를 증설하는 동시에 코어위브와 장기 계약을 체결하면서 외부 컴퓨팅 자원까지 선점하는 움직임이 두드러지고 있다.

메타는 2분기 중 코어위브에 210억달러를 추가로 지출하기로 했다.

코어위브는 생성형 AI 기업 앤트로픽(Anthropic)과도 다년 계약을 체결했다.

퀀트 트레이딩 기업 제인스트리트(Jane Street) 역시 코어위브와 60억달러 규모의 AI 클라우드 계약을 맺었다.

AI 시장의 경쟁력이 단순히 우수한 모델을 만드는 데서 그 모델을 얼마나 빠르고 안정적으로 훈련·운영할 수 있는 컴퓨팅 자원을 확보하느냐로 확대되면서 GPU 공급 능력 자체가 경쟁력이 되고 있는 것이다.

GPU 임대 가격도 이런 수급 상황을 보여준다.

통상 데이터센터 설비가 늘고 반도체 공급이 확대되면 기존 장비의 임대 가격은 떨어질 가능성이 크지만 코어위브가 밝힌 상황은 반대다.

마이크 인트레이터(Mike Intrator) 코어위브 최고경영자(CEO)는 엔비디아 GPU 임대 시장에서 우호적인 가격 흐름이 이어지고 있다고 밝혔다.

인트레이터 CEO는 "블랙웰과 베라 루빈 제품의 가격과 마진이 새로운 최고치를 기록하고 있다"며 "이전 세대 제품의 가격 역시 수년 전 수준 이상을 유지하고 있다"고 말했다.

최신 GPU뿐 아니라 구형 GPU의 가격까지 높은 수준을 유지하고 있다는 의미다.

데이터센터와 GPU 공급이 빠르게 증가하는 상황에서도 임대 가격과 마진이 동시에 오르고 있다는 것은 공급 증가보다 AI 컴퓨팅 수요 증가 속도가 더 빠르다는 의미로 해석할 수 있다.

니틴 아그라왈(Nitin Agrawal) 코어위브 최고재무책임자(CFO)는 데이터센터 구축 과정에서 발생하는 부품 가격 상승분 역시 고객에게 전가하고 있다고 밝혔다.

...

코어위브는 밀려드는 AI 컴퓨팅 수요에 대응하기 위해 데이터센터 투자 규모도 더욱 확대하기로 했다.

올해 예상 자본적지출(CAPEX)은 350억~390억달러다.

지난 5월 제시했던 310억~350억달러보다 40억달러씩 상향됐다.

올해 예상 매출의 약 3배에 달하는 자금을 설비투자에 쏟아붓겠다는 것이다.

...

코어위브는 아직 흑자를 내지 못하고 있으며 2분기 말 기준 대차대조표에 잡힌 부채는 약 350억달러에 달한다.

엔비디아 GPU와 서버, 네트워크 장비 등을 확보하고 데이터센터를 건설하기 위해 대규모 차입에 의존하고 있기 때문이다.

...

빅테크가 자체 데이터센터에 수백억달러를 투자하면서도 동시에 외부 GPU 클라우드와 대규모 장기 계약을 체결하고 최신 GPU 임대 가격과 마진까지 상승하고 있기 때문이다.
